title: The Book of Common Prayer (1549)
hookLine: Cranmer puts worship in English, prayers still used worldwide
carry: cleanse the thoughts of our hearts

lines: DEARLY BELOVED. TILL DEATH US DO PART.
cards: "Dearly beloved, we are gathered together here in the sight of God." "Till death us do part." "Earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust."
Lines like these turn up at weddings and gravesides, in novels and films, and the people saying them don't always know where they came from.
They come from one book, made by the archbishop from yesterday's story, Thomas Cranmer. Henry broke with Rome, but parish services were still in Latin.
Cranmer wanted the whole service in English, said out loud, in a book everyone shared.

teach.b: Common here doesn't mean ordinary. It means shared: one book for every parish, so priest and people pray the same words in the same language. Cranmer didn't write most of it from nothing.

teach.h: OLD LATIN PRAYERS, TURNED INTO ENGLISH.
teach.b: He was a translator at heart, turning old Latin prayers into English with a rhythm that's easy to say together. Before the book, a short Latin prayer was said quietly by the priest as he got ready for Mass.
Cranmer moved it to the opening of the communion service, put it in English, and had it said aloud.

teach.h: CLEANSE THE THOUGHTS, NOT JUST THE HANDS.
teach.b: In the prayer book's later revision it reads: "Almighty God, unto whom all hearts be open, all desires known, and from whom no secrets are hid: Cleanse the thoughts of our hearts by the inspiration of thy Holy Spirit, that we may perfectly love thee, and worthily magnify thy holy Name; through Christ our Lord. Amen."
A prayer of this shape is called a collect: who God is, what we ask, and why. Notice what it asks to have cleaned. Not hands, not deeds: thoughts.
It sounds like the psalm: "Create in me a clean heart, O God."
Not everyone wanted it. In the west of England, some rose up and asked for the old Latin service back. Under Queen Mary it was set aside; later it returned, revised.

Anglican churches in different countries still pray in words from it, and the collect for purity still opens communion in Anglican churches and others. A book that began in an argument became words people say together.

how: Anglicans and Episcopalians pray from prayer books descended from Cranmer's, and in their churches the communion service often begins with the collect for purity, said by the priest or by everyone together.

practice: If you pray, say the collect slowly, a line at a time, with a breath between: Almighty God, unto whom all hearts be open. All desires known. From whom no secrets are hid.
Cleanse the thoughts of our hearts. If you don't, read it as an old poem, and rest on the line that stays.

wordCard.voice: Common Prayer. Cranmer's book of worship in English, common because it is shared, built largely from older Latin prayers turned into words people could say together.

orig.note: Latin: cleanse — the word in the older Latin prayer that Cranmer turned into "cleanse the thoughts of our hearts".

carryVoice: Your line: cleanse the thoughts of our hearts. The week ran from Dirk Willems turning back, through Calvin, Knox and Tyndale's prayer, to Henry's break and this book. A week, done.
